slides.title: 5 kitchen myths you're probably still falling for

slides.myth: Searing a steak seals in the juices.
slides.fact: Searing doesn't make a seal. Seared and unseared steaks lose about the same moisture. It's for the browned flavor, and the real key to juicy meat is not overcooking it.

slides.myth: You should rinse raw chicken before you cook it.
slides.fact: USDA says don't. Rinsing splashes bacteria around your sink and counter, up to 2 to 3 feet away. Cooking to 165°F is what makes chicken safe.
slides.source: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service

slides.myth: Microwaves cook your food from the inside out.
slides.fact: They only reach about an inch into food. The outer layer heats first, then that heat spreads inward. That's why the middle of a thick leftover can stay cold.

slides.myth: All the alcohol cooks off when you add wine to a dish.
slides.fact: Not even close. A USDA study found 4 to 85 percent can remain, depending on the recipe. A quick simmer keeps most of it, and flaming still leaves about 75 percent.
slides.source: USDA Nutrient Data Lab alcohol retention study (1992)

slides.myth: Adding salt makes water boil faster.
slides.fact: A pinch of salt barely changes anything. It raises the boiling point a hair, but a teaspoon in a big pot changes the time by seconds at most. Salt it for taste instead.
